Two projects exploring who systems leave out

MamáMind explores support for mothers after birth. Share A Meal explores how surplus food could reach communities that need it. Both are concept projects focused on access, trust and practical needs.

MamáMind

A team concept for supporting mothers through the first year after birth, with mood journaling, peer support, helpful content and access to therapists.

My role
Research, onboarding screens, style guide
Project type
Collaborative concept, Women Techsters Fellowship
Tools
Figma, Notion
Aligned with
SDG 3, Good Health and Well-being
My contribution
Team research, the onboarding screens, and the style guide.
The key decision
Lead with safe, anonymous support before clinical tools, and keep sensitive features optional.

The problem

Postpartum depression often goes unrecognised. Left unsupported, it can lead to emotional withdrawal, difficulty bonding with the baby, and silence, because asking for help can feel risky.

Our goal was to make the experience feel calm, clear and supportive, even for a mother using it while tired or overwhelmed.

The evidence

We used open-ended survey questions to hear from mothers in their own words and reviewed four existing services: Happify, Postpartum Support International, Headspace and Mayo Clinic.

Our review suggested an opportunity to bring relevant information, peer connection and professional support into a more connected experience.

What we learned, and what we did about it

What the research showed
How the design responded
Many mothers don't recognise postpartum depression, so awareness matters as much as tools.
Mood tracking and journaling help mothers name what they feel, and gentle articles build understanding.
Women want a safe space first, then practical tools.
Anonymous sharing and peer community come before reminders and tracking.
Financial and cultural barriers keep women from professional help.
Articles, affirmations and guided meditation sit alongside therapist booking, so professional help is an option, not a requirement.
Facial-recognition mood tracking is only acceptable if it is optional and consent-led.
Mothers can choose facial recognition or simply write how they feel.

What we designed

The team explored three feature areas in response to the research themes.

Mood tracker

The problem: New mothers find it hard to name what they feel from one moment to the next.

The answer: Mood check-ins, journaling and mood history, with facial recognition proposed as an optional concept feature.

Peer community and articles

The problem: Some mothers may feel isolated or unsure where to find reliable guidance.

The answer: Peer groups and practical articles designed to make support feel approachable.

Therapists, affirmations and meditation

The problem: Stigma or fear of judgement can make seeking support feel difficult.

The answer: Therapist discovery and booking, alongside affirmations and guided meditation.

A decision I'd flag: facial recognition

Facial recognition raises significant questions about privacy, consent, accuracy and sensitive mental-health data. It remains a concept feature, not a validated recommendation. Before any real-world use, I would prioritise research with mothers, clinical input, explicit consent and a clear non-camera alternative. I would also assess whether this feature is necessary at all.

My contribution

  • Research. I contributed to the surveys and review of existing services, and helped translate the findings into design directions.
  • Onboarding screens. Our journey map showed mothers arrive hopeful but cautious about sharing personal details, so the opportunities were simple onboarding, guided setup and skippable non-essential steps. I designed the onboarding screens around that.
  • Style guide. I helped build the style guide, using a soft purple and pink palette, readable type and a distinctive display style to support the intended tone.
  • Collaboration. I collaborated with teammates across African countries and learned to question assumptions rather than design from a single perspective.

Share A Meal

A solo product concept connecting food businesses with NGOs and sponsors to make surplus-food redistribution easier to coordinate and track.

My role
Product designer, solo project
Project type
Solo concept project
Focus
Trust, coordination, food access
Aligned with
SDG 2, Zero Hunger

The problem

The project explores a coordination gap between food businesses with surplus, NGOs seeking food and sponsors who want to support redistribution. Without a clear way to list, claim and track donations, coordination can become difficult and trust harder to maintain.

  • Small businesses lack a system to redistribute surplus food.
  • NGOs don't have consistent access to food supply.
  • Donors lack transparency and trust.

The design opportunity is to make listings, pickups and the use of sponsor funds easier to understand and track.

Choosing a role, donating food, the vendor dashboard, browsing meals, tracking a pickup, and the impact view.

Three users, one loop

  • Vendor
    1. Log surplus food
    2. Publish the listing
    3. Track impact
  • NGO
    1. Browse
    2. Filter
    3. Reserve
    4. Confirm pickup
  • Sponsor
    1. Buy tokens
    2. Allocate to meals
    3. Track meals funded and people reached

A decision: food that expires before pickup

The problem. Surplus food is perishable. If no one collects it in time, the vendor loses trust in the system and a family loses a meal.

My response. I proposed showing expiry information and time remaining, then tracking each donation through clear stages: pending, accepted, picked up and completed. Notifications would help both sides keep track of the handoff.

Tradeoffs I made

Simplicity over intelligence

I prioritised clear, straightforward flows over adding more features, with small-business owners and varying levels of digital confidence in mind.

Trust over full automation

I proposed verifying NGO accounts before enabling claims. This adds friction, but could help build trust and reduce misuse; the process would need to be tested for fairness and ease of access.

What could go wrong

Edge cases I planned for

  • Food expires before pickup
  • NGOs don't show up
  • Low digital literacy among vendors
  • No one claims listed food

How the design responds

  • Time tracking and expiry visibility
  • Clear listing details and timely reminders
  • Simple UI flows
  • A notification system

Proposed AI support

If the core workflow proved useful, future iterations could explore demand forecasting, NGO-to-listing suggestions and pickup planning. These are ideas for further exploration, not implemented features. Any automation should remain explainable and should not replace clear, accessible manual flows.

How I would measure success

Share A Meal is a concept and has not been built or tested. Proposed measures include meals redistributed, the share of listings successfully collected, time to pickup, food waste avoided, sponsor retention and user satisfaction.

The intended outcome is better coordination between food businesses, NGOs and sponsors. These impact claims would need to be assessed through a pilot.

Good design is not just about screens. It's about systems, tradeoffs and real human outcomes, and sometimes the solution is connecting what already exists.

Community advocacy informs how I design

My community work keeps access and inclusion close to my design practice. It has strengthened my interest in creating clearer pathways into technology for women and young people.

Women Techmakers Ambassador since September 2026.

I advocate for teenagers and mothers, including women who feel that motherhood has interrupted their careers. I want more women to see technology as a path that can still be open to them, at different stages of life.
